title: Face with Head-Bandage Emoji 🤕 Meaning: Hurt and Sore
description: 🤕 stands for injuries, headaches and hangovers, plus bruised feelings after a rough day. Here's what the bandaged face means and when to use it over 🤒.
summary: The 🤕 face with head-bandage means someone is hurt. It covers real injuries like a bump, a sprain or a concussion, everyday pain such as a headache or hangover, and emotional knocks like a harsh rejection or a brutal loss. The tone is usually rueful, an ouch rather than an emergency.
meaning: A white bandage wrapped around the skull is how cartoons show a character who has taken a blow, and 🤕 keeps that slapstick flavor. People use it after walking into a door, falling on a run, getting stitches or waking up sore from a hard workout. It reports pain while signaling that the sender will survive.

Headaches are a major use, simply because the bandage is on the head. Migraines, tension headaches and the pounding of a hangover all get 🤕, often on its own as a morning-after message. For that reason it has become one of the stock hangover emojis alongside the nauseated and woozy faces.

The emoji also describes damage that is not physical. A team that lost badly, a person who was turned down, a student who just saw their grade: all of them might send 🤕 to say that one hurt. It suits wounded pride particularly well because it looks a little sheepish.

Finally, it is used toward other people as sympathy. Replying 🤕 to a friend's story about a fall says ouch, that sounds painful. It is softer than a crying face and acknowledges the injury without making a big scene about it, which suits the kind of mishap the friend is already half laughing at.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: It is a fast way to explain that you are out of action. After a minor accident, a dental procedure or a rough night, 🤕 tells friends what state you are in. Most replies ask what happened, so expect to follow it with the story.

contexts.label: In sports
contexts.body: Fans post it when a player goes down injured or lands on the injury list, and athletes use it themselves for knocks and recovery updates. It also labels a heavy defeat, as in the team took a beating. In fantasy leagues it is shorthand for an injured pick.

contexts.label: After a night out
contexts.body: The morning message 🤕 with no words is understood almost everywhere as I drank too much. It tends to be self-mocking. Paired with a drink emoji or a question about what happened last night, it becomes a full confession and an invitation to fill in the gaps.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: It is acceptable for explaining a minor injury or a headache that is slowing you down. Using it for a bruising meeting or a rejected proposal is fine with peers. Do not use it to joke about workplace accidents, which are taken seriously for good reason.

examples.text: Tripped on the curb in front of everyone 🤕
examples.meaning: The sender fell, is a bit hurt and mostly embarrassed.
A hangover report, said with regret that will not last.

examples.meaning: They have a bad headache and will be offline.

examples.text: She said she just wants to be friends 🤕
examples.meaning: A rejection stung, and the sender is nursing hurt feelings.
Sympathy for someone else who has been injured.
The defeat was painful and a little humiliating.

combos.meaning: Hungover and blaming last night's drinks.
Patched up after a small injury, or slowly recovering.
Emotionally hurt, typically after a breakup or rejection.
An injury serious enough for the emergency room or a doctor.

confusedWith.difference: 🤒 is sick with a fever or infection. 🤕 is injured or in pain. A cold calls for the thermometer; a sprained ankle, a headache or a hangover calls for the bandage.
😵 is knocked out, stunned or overwhelmed, with X-shaped eyes. 🤕 is conscious and aching afterward. Think of 😵 as the impact and 🤕 as the recovery.
🥴 describes being drunk or dazed in the moment. 🤕 describes the consequences the next morning, or any pain that has a clear cause.

avoid: Do not use it to make light of someone's serious injury or head trauma.
Avoid it as your only message after a real accident if people may worry; tell them you are okay.
Skip it when someone is grieving, since it frames pain as minor and slightly comic.
design: A yellow face with a frown and pained or half-closed eyes, its head wrapped in a white gauze bandage that usually crosses the forehead at an angle. Vendors differ in small ways: some cover one eye or eyebrow with the wrap, some show a knot or clip, and the mouth ranges from a slight frown to a wince.

faqs.a: Very often. A solitary 🤕 sent the morning after a party is commonly understood as a pounding head from drinking. It is not the only meaning, though. Any headache or injury fits, so check what the person was doing the night before.

faqs.q: What does 🤕 mean from a guy or girl after an argument?
faqs.a: It usually means they feel hurt by what was said. It is a softer, less confrontational way of admitting that than typing it out, and it often works as an opening for an apology or a calmer follow-up conversation.

faqs.q: Can I use 🤕 for emotional pain?
faqs.a: Yes, for the everyday kind: rejection, embarrassment, a tough loss, criticism that stung. For deep grief or serious distress it is too light, and the broken heart, crying faces or plain words are a better fit.

faqs.q: When was the head-bandage emoji released?
faqs.a: It was approved in Unicode 8.0 and added to emoji keyboards in 2015, the same year as the thermometer face, the nerd face and the hugging face. It is supported on every current platform.
